prompt: Finance was not built for you to make a living out of it

props.quote: You start from the riskiest side of a very risky business already.
body: Finance was born to protect savings. Money moves from saving, to investing, to growing capital, and only at the very end to speculation. Every step up is riskier.
Retail traders jump straight to speculation, usually with leverage. That's why you need the right expectations and a real statistical edge before anything else.

points.title: Risk to reward
points.text: What you risk on a trade vs. what you can win.

points.title: Win rate
points.text: The share of trades that end as winners.

points.title: Profit factor
points.text: Total wins ÷ total losses. Above 1 means profitable.

prompt: Order the uses of money from safest to riskiest

props.explain: Finance starts with saving and investing. Speculation, where retail traders start, is the riskiest step.

prompt: How much can even the best in the world make?
Win rate and reward-to-risk trade off

body: Every strategy has two numbers: how much it makes when it wins compared with what it risks (reward-to-risk, or R), and how often it wins (win rate).
The further your take profit, the bigger each win, but the less often price gets there. So you need a lower win rate to break even, and you'll also win less often.

points.title: Above the line
points.text: Win more often than break-even and the profit factor goes above 1.

points.title: Profit factor
points.text: Add up every win, add up every loss, divide wins by losses.

prompt: Place a 1:2 strategy exactly on the break-even line
Andrea's 10 trades, each risking 1 to make 2

props.question: Winners pay +2, losers −1. What's the profit factor (total wins ÷ total losses)?
props.correct: 5 wins × 2 = 10, 5 losses × 1 = 5, so 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Profitable while winning only half the time.
props.hint: Add up all the wins (5 × 2), add up all the losses (5 × 1), then divide wins by losses.

prompt: Three ways to trade

props.quote: Start with a documented edge and clear rules, then build your screen time.
body: Once you know what an edge looks like, there are three ways to trade it. Each has its own strength and its own trap.

points.title: Algorithmic
points.text: A coded bot follows the rules with no emotions. The trap is overfitting: tuning it so hard on past data that it fails on new data.

points.title: Discretionary
points.text: You trade by hand and your read of the market is the edge. The hardest path: few succeed, but the winners win big.

points.title: Hybrid
points.text: Rules researched and documented like an algo, but you place the trades. Andrea's recommended place to start.

prompt: Algo, discretionary or hybrid?

buckets.label: Algorithmic
buckets.hint: A coded bot executes the rules

items.label: Risk of overfitting to past data
Your read of the market is the edge
Few succeed, but the winners win big
Trade a documented edge with clear rules, manually

props.explain: Algos are objective but can overfit and decay. Discretion is the hardest path with the biggest upside. Hybrid gives beginners clear rules plus screen time.

prompt: Everything you need as a trader

props.quote: It's not a get-rich-quick type of thing.
body: Trading needs more than a laptop and an internet connection. It needs real knowledge, honest time, a portfolio of strategies, capital that doesn't come from your rent, and the right tools.

points.title: Knowledge
points.text: Fundamentals & macro, technical analysis, data analysis.

points.title: Time
points.text: Pick a style that fits your schedule.

points.title: Strategy
points.text: Ideally several, diversified.

points.title: Capital
points.text: Real, demo, or a prop firm.

points.title: Platform
points.text: Broker or prop firm + a trading terminal.

points.title: Journal & risk manager
points.text: Track your metrics, protect your account.

prompt: Pick a style that fits your time

body: Your style has to fit your week, not the other way around. If your time depends on someone else, like a boss or your own business, pick a style that doesn't need you at the screen at fixed hours.
Andrea's advice is to go step by step: build cash flow and save, invest passively, trade part-time, and only go full-time once you see real signs of success.

points.title: Investing and swing trading
points.text: A few hours a week or less. Fits a job or a business.

points.title: Day trading and scalping
points.text: 3–4 hours a day, often at the New York open. Fits someone who controls their hours.

points.title: Running algos seriously
points.text: Also hours every day: research, testing and monitoring.

prompt: How much time does each style need?

buckets.label: A few hours a week or less

props.explain: With a job or a business, swing trading or investing fits. Day trading, scalping and serious algo work need hours every day.

prompt: Andrea's path into the markets

props.bottomLabel: Later, only with signs of success
props.explain: Go gradually: cash flow first, then passive investing, then part-time trading. Going all-in without capital, knowledge or a strategy is a recipe for disaster.

prompt: How a prop firm pays you

body: A prop firm lends you its capital. You pay a fee for a challenge, and if you hit its profit target without breaking its risk rules, you trade a funded account.
You keep a share of the profits, called the split. Most people who buy a challenge fail, and their fees pay for the few who get paid.

points.title: Profit
points.text: Account size × your return. $100,000 × 5% = $5,000.

points.title: Your payout
points.text: Profit × your split. $5,000 × 80% = $4,000.

prompt: How a prop-firm challenge pays out
The tools of the trade

body: Besides a broker or prop firm, you need a trading terminal. Andrea uses a different one for each style.

points.title: DeepCharts
points.text: Order flow on futures. Built for day trading and scalping.

points.title: TradingView
points.text: Easy, clean charting. Good for swing trading and macro.

points.title: MultiCharts
points.text: Backtesting and automation. Built for algo trading.

prompt: Match the platform to the trading style

props.explain: DeepCharts for order-flow day trading, TradingView for swing and macro charting, MultiCharts for algos.

prompt: Break-even with a wider target

props.question: Your strategy risks 1 to make 3. What win rate do you need just to break even?
props.correct: 1 ÷ (1 + 3) = 25%. The further the target, the less often you need to win, and the less often you will.
props.hint: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + R), with R = 3.

help.hint: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + R), where R is what you make for every 1 you risk. Here R = 3.

prompt: Profit factor at 1:1

props.question: 10 trades at 1:1. Six win (+1 each), four lose (−1 each). What's the profit factor?
props.hint: Total wins (6 × 1) divided by total losses (4 × 1).

help.hint: Profit factor = total won ÷ total lost. Add up the six +1s, add up the four −1s, then divide.

prompt: What happens?

rows.label: Move your take profit further away → your win rate
Move your take profit closer → your win rate
Optimise a strategy too hard on past data → odds it works live
rows.why: That's overfitting: great on old data, poor on new data.

props.explain: Win rate and reward-to-risk always trade off against each other.

help.hint: A target further away is reached less often. And a strategy tuned too tightly to old data learns its noise, not its edge.

buckets.label: Day trading the New York open

items.label: Full-time employee with a fixed schedule
Business owner who's needed all day
Freelancer who controls their own hours

props.explain: If your time depends on someone else, trade styles that don't need you at the screen at fixed hours.

help.hint: Ask who controls each person's hours. If someone else does, they need a style that doesn't need them at the screen at fixed times.

prompt: Prop-firm payout

props.question: You make 8% on a $100,000 funded account with a 90% profit split. What's your payout?

help.hint: Profit = account × return. Your payout = profit × your split.

prompt: Rank the yearly returns

props.explain: Even the record holder makes ~60% a year, nowhere near the “10% a month” gurus promise.

help.hint: Compare a yearly percentage for each: the stock market's long-run average, the best-known value investor, and the record-holding quant fund.

links.label: S&P 500 average returns and historical performance

prompt: Who, what, how and why

props.quote: The price you see on your charts is simply the last transaction between a buyer and a seller.
body: Prices move through order flow: a stream of buy and sell orders. Behind it are smart money and slow money (banks, funds, central banks), market makers who quote both sides and earn the spread, small money, and retail: us.
Big players can't buy everything at once. They split huge orders into small ones over hours or days, which is why trends persist and order flow is autocorrelated.

prompt: Who's who in the market?

items.label: Quotes bid and ask, earns the spread

props.explain: Banks, funds, governments and central banks are big money. Market makers stay neutral and earn the spread. Under ~$100M is small money, and retail is the smallest of all.

prompt: Passive or aggressive?

items.label: Buy limit at 59 while price is 60
Market buy, filled at the best ask
Market sell into the best bid

props.explain: Passive orders name their price and wait for someone to come. Aggressive orders accept the best available price to get filled now, and that's what moves price.

prompt: You're the big buyer now. Find the largest market buy that keeps slippage under 0.03%

help.hint: Each ask level costs more. Slippage stays tiny until you eat into the pricier levels, so push the size up until it only just stays under 0.03%.

prompt: Why is this money moving?

items.label: IKEA locks in next year's wood price with futures
Market maker offsetting too much exposure

props.explain: Preservation, growth and hedging flows are the big, predictable ones. Speculative flows are the least predictable and drive FOMO and bubbles.

prompt: Money today is created through debt

props.quote: Debt, or credit, is the only way new money is created nowadays.
body: Since the end of the gold standard in 1971, money is fiat: it's worth something because we trust it. New money is created when governments and companies issue bonds, and when banks make loans.
A bond is an IOU with an issuer, a nominal value, a maturity and a yield. Most of the money in financial markets sits in bonds.

points.title: Credit rating
points.text: Riskier borrowers must pay more.

points.title: Term premium
points.text: Lend for longer, get paid more.

points.title: Inflation expectations
points.text: Higher expected inflation, higher yield.

points.title: Central bank rates
points.text: Bonds must beat the risk-free rate.

prompt: Put the history of money in order

items: Banks hold gold and issue banknotes
props.explain: Coins, then banknotes backed by gold, then the end of convertibility in 1971 and today's fiat, debt-based money.

prompt: Investment grade or junk?

props.explain: AAA to BBB is investment grade. BB and below is junk, and D means default: the borrower couldn't pay.

prompt: Shape a normal yield curve
What happens to the yield a lender demands?

rows.label: The issuer's credit rating is downgraded
The loan is for 30 years instead of 3 months
Inflation is expected to fall
The central bank cuts interest rates

props.explain: Yield = credit risk + term premium + inflation expectations + central bank rates.

prompt: A stock is a piece of a company

props.quote: Markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.
body: A company's capital is split into shares. After an IPO those shares trade publicly as stocks. Owning them gives you a share of the company and of its profits.
People buy stocks for two reasons: growth (the company becomes worth more) and income (dividends). That makes the stock market a risk-on, sentiment-driven market.

prompt: Split the profits between the owners
Match the index

buckets.label: Top 500 US stocks by market cap
Top 100 on the Nasdaq, mostly tech

props.explain: Indices pick the stocks for you. You can trade them through ETFs, futures or options.

prompt: Who suffers most in a recession?

props.explain: In a downturn people stop buying new iPhones but still buy bread at Walmart, and money flows into safe havens like Treasuries.

prompt: Which side of the order book?

items.label: Buy limit below the current price
Sell limit above the current price

props.explain: Passive buyers rest on the bid, passive sellers on the ask. Aggressive orders cross over to them.

help.hint: The bid is what buyers are willing to pay, the ask is what sellers want. A buyer waiting below the price joins the buyers.

prompt: Cause and effect

rows.label: A huge market buy sweeps the ask side → price
rows.why: It eats through sell offers at higher and higher prices.

rows.label: A huge market sell hits the bids → price
rows.why: It fills against buyers at lower and lower prices.

rows.label: Stocks crash → bond prices
rows.why: Money flees risk into safe-haven bonds.

rows.label: An issuer's credit rating is upgraded → the yield it pays

props.explain: Aggressive orders move price, and money rotates between risk and safety.

help.hint: A market order takes whatever is resting on the other side, one price level at a time. In a crash, money runs toward the safest assets. A safer issuer can pay less to borrow.

prompt: Dividends

props.question: A company earns $1,000,000 net and reinvests $200,000. You own 10%. What's your dividend?
props.hint: Subtract what's reinvested, then take your ownership share.

help.hint: Only the profit that isn't reinvested is paid out. Your dividend is your ownership share of that payout.

prompt: Normal or inverted yield curve?

items.label: Long maturities yield more than short ones
Typically appears when rate hikes are expected

props.explain: Normally you're paid more to lend for longer. Expected hikes push short yields above long ones.

help.hint: Lending for longer is riskier, so you're normally paid more for it. When the market expects hikes, short-term yields jump first.

prompt: Growth or income?

items.label: Expecting more investors to pile in later
Tesla, for years without paying dividends
A share of the yearly profits

props.explain: People buy stocks for growth, for income, or both.

help.hint: Ask where the money comes from: the share price going up, or cash the company pays you.

prompt: From founders to the stock market

items: Founders put capital into the company
The capital is split into shares
IPO: shares are offered to the public
Shares trade on the exchange as stocks
props.explain: A share becomes a stock once it's listed and trades publicly after the IPO.

help.hint: A company exists before it is public. It only becomes a stock once it's listed and anyone can trade it.

unit: Unit 3: Macro & the flow of money
prompt: Debt creates the economic cycle

props.quote: The markets will always try to anticipate what the economy will do.
body: When a bank lends, it creates new money. Borrowing lets everyone spend more, then repaying forces everyone to spend less: leveraging and deleveraging. That's the 5–7 year economic cycle.
Central banks have two mandates: keep inflation around 2% and maximise employment. Their main tool is the interest rate.

points.title: GDP
points.text: How much wealth the economy creates.

points.title: Inflation
points.text: How fast prices rise. Target: ~2%.

points.title: Employment
points.text: How many people have jobs.

unit: Unit 3: Macro & the flow of money
prompt: Inflation, by the cup

props.question: A coffee cost $1.00 last year and costs $1.10 today. What's the inflation rate?
props.correct: ($1.10 − $1.00) ÷ $1.00 = 10%. That's five times the 2% central banks aim for.
props.hint: Divide the price increase by the old price: $0.10 ÷ $1.00.

unit: Unit 3: Macro & the flow of money
prompt: Currencies follow interest rates

props.quote: Interest rates from central banks are the main driver of the forex market.
body: Forex is trading one currency against another. EUR/USD at 1.08 means €1 buys $1.08. If the dollar weakens or the euro strengthens, the number goes up.
Global money parks where bonds pay more. So the gap between two central banks' rates, driven by inflation and unemployment data, sets the trend of a pair.

rows.why: Dollar bonds pay more → demand for dollars.

rows.label: USD/JPY: Fed cuts, Bank of Japan starts hiking
rows.why: The rate gap shrinks, so money flows back to yen.

props.explain: The numerator over the denominator: whatever strengthens the first currency lifts the pair.

unit: Unit 3: Macro & the flow of money
prompt: Gold competes with bonds

props.quote: Whenever real yields go down, gold goes up.
body: Since 1971 gold has mostly been an inflation hedge and a store of value. "War = gold up" is more myth than a reliable rule.
Bonds are the other inflation hedge. When the real yield (bond yield minus inflation) is high, money prefers bonds. When it falls, money flows into gold.
Real commodities like oil, cocoa or lithium follow one thing: supply (production) vs. demand (consumption).

unit: Unit 3: Macro & the flow of money
prompt: Money doesn't burn, it moves

props.quote: It didn't really burn. It just went into a place where it was expecting a better or safer return.
body: Economic data comes out every month. Analysts and algorithms at every bank turn it into forecasts for the next 6–9 months, and money is re-allocated between markets, split into small orders that move price.
Analysing how money moves between bonds, forex, commodities, stocks and gold is called intermarket analysis.

prompt: Two research-backed strategies

Post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD): after a positive earnings surprise, institutional buying makes the stock drift higher for weeks. Wait for a retest of the gap, then target 1:1 to 1:2.

help.hint: Look at the end of the downtrend: a small red candle, then a green one whose body is bigger and covers it completely.

prompt: Is each market trending or ranging?

help.hint: Trends keep making new highs (or new lows). Ranges keep bouncing between the same two levels.

prompt: Tune the moving average until it gives 3 or fewer crossover signals

help.hint: Short averages hug price and flip sides often. Slide toward a longer period to smooth out the noise.

prompt: Find the biggest market buy that keeps slippage under 0.03%

help.hint: Each ask level costs more. Slippage stays tiny until you eat into the pricier levels, so push the size up until it only just stays under 0.03%.

prompt: Your rule: only buy a breakout after a candle closes above resistance. What do you do?

help.hint: Look at where the last candle closed, not how high its wick went.

prompt: Price just broke out. Drag your stop loss and take profit to follow the plan.

help.hint: Put the stop just under 108. Your risk is entry minus stop; set the target at least twice that distance above the entry.

prompt: Use the lab to size your position

help.hint: Set the stop to 40 pips, then raise the risk until the position reads 0.5 lots.

prompt: Find a system that wins less than 40% of the time but still has an expectancy of at least +0.2R

help.hint: Expectancy = win rate × reward − loss rate × 1. Fewer wins means each win must pay more: lower the win rate, then raise the reward.

prompt: Review this trader's last 10 trades

help.hint: Add up every R in the log, then divide by the number of trades.
